focus_areas: HTTP /v1/* OpenAI API forward & per-model ACL (handler.go, acl.go, trusted.go, middleware.go)
Routing / model body / multipart and body caps (router.go, load.go)
etcd source & config trust boundary (source.go, etcdclient.go, disabled.go, config.go)

findings.title: X-Model header vs body model confusion lets a client bypass the per-model ACL
findings.description: ModelRouter.Route (router.go:157) reads the client-supplied X-Model header and uses it as the routed model for both ACL and backend selection (router.go:200-206 for JSON, router.go:233-259 for multipart). The request body is read and buffered but the `model` field inside it is ignored for routing. The full original body is then forwarded to the chosen backend byte-for-byte (handler.go:318 copyHeaders, handler.go:303-306 replays route.Body; multipart replayed verbatim too). Handler.ServeHTTP runs the ACL against route.Model, which is the header value (handler.go:222-233), while the backend executes the `model` field that remains in the forwarded body. So a client can attach X-Model for an allowed model to satisfy routing/ACL, while embedding a different, restricted model in the body; the proxy forwards the body unchanged and the backend serves the restricted model.
findings.exploit_scenario: Client sends POST /v1/chat/completions with X-Model: public-model and a JSON body {"model":"secret-paid-model",...}. The proxy authenticates/ACL-checks against public-model (allowed), forwards the raw body with model=secret-paid-model to the public-model backend, which serves it. The ACL intended to protect secret-paid-model is never enforced because the body model is never inspected. The same holds for multipart audio uploads (X-Model vs multipart `model` form field).
findings.recommendation: Do not let a client-supplied header silently override the body model for authorization. Parse the body first, derive the effective model from the body `model` field (or a fully-trusted internal header, not a client-spoofable one), and ACL-check the exact model the backend will execute. If X-Model support is required, treat a body/header mismatch as an error or re-write the body model before forwarding so routing == backend execution.
findings.confidence_reason: The mismatch between the model used for routing/ACL (header, router.go:157/200/233) and the model actually executed by the backend (raw body forwarded unchanged at handler.go:303-318) is unambiguous from the code; independent scoring rated it 8/10.

findings.title: etcd watch drops a model's ACL on an invalid PUT while retaining stale backends
findings.description: In EtcdSource.watch (source.go:158-167), on EventTypePut parseKV returns (nil, nil, false) when the new value is invalid (non-JSON, empty backends, no valid api_base). The `if ok` guard (source.go:160-162) leaves nextM[name] pointing at the previously-loaded backends (stale), but the `else { delete(nextA, name) }` branch (source.go:165-167) unconditionally removes the model's ACL rule because acl==nil on parse failure. The stale backends therefore remain routable while the ACL entry is dropped, and ACLConfig.Check (acl.go:69-87) fails open for models with no rule, so the previously restricted model becomes reachable without authorization.
findings.exploit_scenario: An account with etcd write access clobbers /.../models/<restricted-model> with a malformed value (or a value with one empty api_base that invalidates the whole entry). The proxy keeps serving that model from the old backend list but clears its ACL, so a caller with no matching allow rule is still granted access (allow-by-default).
findings.recommendation: Make watch updates atomic and fail-closed: on a parse failure, either drop the model entirely (both nextM and nextA) or keep both the old backends and the old ACL together; never remove the ACL while retaining routable backends. Reject or quarantine malformed values instead of partially applying them.
findings.confidence_reason: The asymmetric handling (keep nextM, delete nextA on failure) is directly visible in source.go:160-167 and clearly interacts with the allow-by-default Check at acl.go:69; impact depends on a malformed write reaching etcd.

findings.title: etcd-derived api_base URLs are contacted with client headers (incl. Authorization) forwarded, enabling SSRF and credential forwarding when the etcd prefix is writable
findings.description: EtcdSource.parseKV (source.go:189-206) turns api_base strings from the etcd models prefix into *url.URL with no scheme/host allowlist via url.Parse (source.go:195). The health checker GETs <backend>/v1/models (health.go:277-325) and Handler.tryOnce forwards each request to the backend with all client headers cloned (handler.go:318 via copyHeaders at handler.go:685-692), including Authorization and X-User-Id, and joins the client path onto the backend base (handler.go:308-310). A poisoned api_base therefore makes the proxy issue outbound HTTP (and forward the requesting client's Authorization) to an arbitrary internal host. Exploitation requires an account able to write the inference etcd prefix (control-plane, threat T6) and is compounded by the plaintext etcd fallback when TLS env is unset (etcdclient.go:63-69).
findings.exploit_scenario: A writer sets api_base for a model to an internal admin service or 127.0.0.1:<internal-port>. A legitimate client calls that model; the proxy forwards the full request, including the client's Authorization header, to the attacker-chosen internal host, enabling internal recon and credential/data exfiltration.
findings.recommendation: Schema-validate api_base in the etcd source (allow only http/https against an allowlisted host set), enforce etcd mTLS so only trusted writers can set api_base, and avoid forwarding sensitive client headers (Authorization) to untrusted backends. Treat etcd writers as a security boundary.
findings.confidence_reason: Mechanism grounded in source.go:195 and handler.go:318, but exploitation requires etcd write access, currently limited to trusted control-plane nodes, so it is credible but contingent.

findings.title: ACL is allow-by-default for models with no matching rule
findings.description: ACLConfig.Check (acl.go:69-87) only denies when an explicit ACLDeny entry matches. If the requested model has no ACL rule (acl.go:73-75), or none of the rule's entries match the caller (fall-through at acl.go:77-86), Check returns nil = allow. The main API listener is bound to loopback (main.go:152; default listen 127.0.0.1:4001) and TrustedHeadersMiddleware strips spoofed X-User-Id from non-trusted peers (trusted.go:21-28, DefaultTrustedProxies = loopback), so the direct no-identity path is mitigated in the managed deployment. The residual gap is an authenticated request through nginx that matches no ACL entry for the requested model: it is allowed, and safety depends on the listener staying loopback-bound.
findings.exploit_scenario: An authenticated external user requests a model that has ACL entries, but the caller's user/groups match none of them; Check matches no entry and allows the request. If Listen is ever overridden to a non-loopback address, any cluster host that can reach it is served with no identity at all (allow-by-default).
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: no-match should deny for any model that has at least one ACL rule (and ideally for any known model), verify every routable model has an explicit allow, keep the API listener loopback-bound, and require authentication for any non-loopback peer.
findings.confidence_reason: The allow-by-default code path is unambiguous, but the highest-impact direct-access vector is mitigated by the loopback bind; what remains is the per-model/per-identity coverage gap that is harder to verify statically.

findings.title: etcd client silently falls back to plaintext when TLS env vars are unset
findings.description: etcdTLSConfig (etcdclient.go:63-93) returns (nil, nil) — i.e. no TLS — whenever ETCD_CACERT, ETCD_CERT and ETCD_KEY are all absent (etcdclient.go:67-69), and the code then dials the etcd endpoints (default http://localhost:2379) over plaintext. There is no failure mode forcing TLS, so a misconfigured/under-provisioned deployment attaches to etcd without encryption or server-certificate verification. The threat model flags as an open question whether etcd mTLS is enforced in this environment; this fallback guarantees it isn't, purely on the basis of environment absence.
findings.exploit_scenario: If ETCD_* env vars are not provisioned, the proxy reads and writes the ACL/model source in cleartext (and skips CA pinning, with RootCAs being nil at etcdclient.go:83 when only CACERT is missing). An on-path or LAN attacker with access to the etcd traffic path could read model/ACL data or spoof updates, and channel failure would not be detected.
findings.recommendation: Require an explicit TLS mode (e.g. default to tls/verify when endpoints are reachable over the network), fail startup when mTLS is expected but not configured, and always load a CA when the endpoint is not loopback. Enforce etcd mTLS end-to-end per the threat model rather than leaving it to optional env.
findings.confidence_reason: The plaintext fallback is unambiguous in the code, but whether it is exploitable depends on deployment (whether ETCD_* are set) and on the network placement of etcd, which is not fully determinable statically.

findings.title: Unauthenticated /metrics on the dedicated listener exposes backend URLs and model inventory cluster-wide
findings.description: The metrics registry exposes label values containing full backend URLs and model names (metrics.go:51-93: label 'backend' = URL strings, 'model' = model names), plus live inflight/state gauges. When metrics_listen is set, /metrics is served on a dedicated separate listener (main.go:154-158, default inference_proxy_metrics_port 4010 on all interfaces for cross-host Prometheus scraping) with no auth and no firewall restriction visible in the repo. The main API listener is loopback-bound, but this metrics port remains intentionally cross-host-reachable, so any cluster-internal host can enumerate the backend fleet and model topology and observe real-time routing state.
findings.exploit_scenario: Any cluster-internal host with network reach to the target's :4010 issues GET /metrics and reads backend URLs, model names, retry counts, and inflight gauges — effectively a live service inventory that also informs which hosts/ports are worth probing.
findings.recommendation: Restrict :4010 at the firewall to the Prometheus/observability hosts, add scrape auth/token, or run a scrape target that rewrites sensitive labels; keep /metrics off any public path and confirm nginx never proxies it.
findings.confidence_reason: The disclosure surface is real and code-grounded, but impact is informational and partially intentional (Prometheus needs these labels); the risk is the open reachability with no ACL.

findings.title: /healthz echoes backend URLs, probe error strings, and model names
findings.description: writeHealthz (handler.go:418-529) serializes every backend URL, state, last-check timestamp, and probe error string into the JSON response (handler.go:449-457, 485-487), and per-model entries include backend URL lists. The handler is served on the main listener (handler.go:140-149), which is loopback-bound (main.go:152), so in the managed deployment it is only reachable from the node itself. Impact is therefore limited to local disclosure of internal URL inventory and error detail, and is largely risk-accepted operational telemetry.
findings.exploit_scenario: If the /healthz path is ever proxied by nginx or the listener is rebound off-loopback, any reachable host can read backend URLs and raw probe error strings (which can leak internal hostnames/paths). Scope today is local-only.
findings.recommendation: Redact backend URLs and raw error strings from /healthz in any externally reachable context (return counts/states only), restrict the listener, and confirm nginx never proxies /healthz.
findings.confidence_reason: The disclosure is real but currently mitigated by the loopback bind; risk materializes only if the listener is widened or the path is proxied.

findings.title: Passthrough mode routes with an empty model, so per-model ACL is never enforced
findings.description: PassthroughRouter.Route returns a RouteResult with Model unset/empty (router.go:95-97, leaving Model as "" since only Candidates is populated). Handler.ServeHTTP then calls acl.Check(route.Model, ...) which is acl.Check("", ...) (handler.go:222-233). ACLConfig.Check first looks up a.Models[""] (acl.go:73-75); there is no empty-key rule, so it returns nil = allow. Consequently in passthrough mode no per-model ACL is applied at the proxy at all, since the body is never parsed and the ACL always fails open on the empty model.
findings.exploit_scenario: A deployment running in passthrough/single-backend mode with an ACL configured achieves no authorization: any request to the single backend is forwarded regardless of the model in the body, because the ACL check against the empty routed model trivially succeeds.
findings.recommendation: In passthrough mode, either disallow ACL configuration (fail fast with an error), enforce a single-model allowlist, or parse the body model before forwarding so the ACL can be applied.
findings.confidence_reason: The empty-model routing (router.go:95-97) and fail-open Check on an empty key (acl.go:73) are clear, but passthrough mode is a narrower deployment path and ACL impact depends on the operator choosing to run passthrough with ACLs.

findings.title: CLI-discovered model IDs are written as etcd keys after only weak validation
findings.description: modelsAdd with no explicit model calls discoverModels(apiBase) (cli.go:166), which GETs <api-base>/v1/models and extracts model IDs from the backend response (cli.go:518-549). Each returned ID is validated only by validateModelName (cli.go:134-142), which rejects empty and "://"-containing names, then written to etcd as key = prefix + model (cli.go:203). There is no restriction on control characters, separators, or length, so a backend (or a TLS-intercepting/untrusted api-base) emitting a crafted ID such as one with a slash, newline, or very long value can influence the etcd key namespace and persisted data. This is operator-triggered but the model IDs originate from a network endpoint, not the operator's terminal, so the input is only weakly trusted.
findings.exploit_scenario: An operator runs `local-ai-proxy models add <api-base>` against a backend that reports a polluting model ID (e.g. containing path separators or oversized). The ID is persisted to etcd without sanitization, creating unexpected keys/values that a downstream consumer may parse ambiguously.
findings.recommendation: Apply a strict allowlist charset/length for model IDs before persisting (no control chars, '/', '\\', or reserved etcd-key delimiters), and reject/redact IDs that fail validation rather than writing them.
findings.confidence_reason: Validation is demonstrably minimal (cli.go:134-142), but the impact is an operator-facing CLI with network-derived input and no strong downstream consumer identified, so it is speculative/low signal.

findings.title: Broad /v1/* path forwarding and blocklist header pass-through expose backend endpoints and allow header injection
findings.description: Any path under /v1/ is accepted and forwarded verbatim to the chosen backend (handler.go:308-310 builds target from r.URL.Path; upstream routed at handler.go:312-318), and the client's complete header set is copied through except hop-by-hop, via copyHeaders (handler.go:318, 685-692). There is no per-backend allowlist of downstream paths, methods, or forwarded headers. Backend response bodies are streamed verbatim (handler.go:347-350). A client can reach backend endpoints the gateway never intended to expose and inject arbitrary headers (including X-Forwarded-For) into backend requests; backend-specific impact depends on how the downstream interprets those paths/headers.
findings.exploit_scenario: An authenticated client sends /v1/admin/... through the proxy; the /v1/* prefix check passes and it is forwarded to the backend, which may treat it as an admin call. The client can also set X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1 to spoof trust for backends that key access decisions off forwarded-for.
findings.recommendation: Replace blocklist header forwarding with an explicit allowlist (e.g. Accept, Accept-Encoding, Authorization, Content-Type, User-Agent, X-User-Id, OpenAI-*) and add a per-backend allowlist of permitted /v1/* subpaths and methods; strip X-Forwarded-* unless it is regenerated by a trusted proxy.
findings.confidence_reason: The no-allowlist forwarding is unambiguous, but concrete impact depends on backend-specific interpretation of forwarded headers/paths, which is not determinable statically; hence low signal.
